newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani voters trickle to the polls.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani voters trickle to the polls.

text.p: Pakistanis began voting on Monday in an election forced by President Farooq Leghari's dismissal of Benazir Bhutto on corruption charges, but the early turn-out was low.
Few voters showed up when polling stations opened in fine weather at 7:00 a.m. (0200 GMT), an hour earlier than usual due to the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan.
Bhutto, who went to vote at 8:00 a.m. in a primary school in her village of Naudero, in Sindh province, was visibly surprised to find that she was the first to cast a ballot there.
"People are voting for the arrow because they want stability, they want democracy," she said, referring to the election symbol of her Pakistan People's Party (PPP).
"The PPP stands for economic reform," she said before visiting the graves of her father Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and her brothers Murtaza and Shahnawaz in Garhi Khuda Bux village.
She scattered rose petals on their graves and distributed 100-rupee ($2.50) banknotes to about 150 supporters there.
Ghinwa Bhutto, Lebanese-born widow of the slain Murtaza and now leader of the splinter PPP faction that he founded, was also the first person to vote in her Larkana constituency.
In Karachi, troops guarded polling stations and paramilitary rangers patrolled the streets of the volatile port city.
Two supporters of the breakaway Haqiqi faction of the Mohajir National Movement (MQM) were wounded by gunfire in Moosa Colony of District Central overnight.
Baba Ghori, a spokesman for the MQM's London-based leader Altaf Hussain, complained that voters were being intimidated.

"We are not happy with security arrangements," he said. "At most polling stations, election officers did not show up in the first hour and in the sensitive areas of Landhi and Shah Faisal Colony Haqiqi men are firing to stop MQM voters from going out."
Ghori said the MQM had appealed to the authorities to tighten security, but had received no response.

In Islamabad, one young voter, Mohammad Agha, waved a key-ring in the shape of a tiger, electoral symbol of Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (PML). "That's who I'm going to vote for and so is everyone else," he said.
The 36,415 polling stations, guarded by police and 250,000 troops on election duty, will stay open until 4:00 p.m. (1100 GMT), with results expected late in the evening.
The main fight pits the PML, fielding 177 National Assembly candidates, against Bhutto's PPP, with 161 candidates.

Ex-cricketer Imran Khan's Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) has put up 132 candidates, Ghinwa Bhutto's PPP-Shaheed Bhutto faction 66 and the MQM 55. Others are from smaller parties or are standing as independents.
Leghari promised in an address to the nation on Sunday night that the polls would be free, fair and open.
Bhutto rejected any notion she might agree to leave Pakistan to escape possible prosecution for corruption.
"The question does not arise of my seeking asylum in Britain or anywhere else," she told Reuters at her farmhouse in Naudero.

She was responding to a report in London's Sunday Times, which quoted senior Pakistani government sources as saying that to avoid a sensitive trial, possible corruption charges against Bhutto and her jailed husband Asif Ali Zardari could be dropped if she agreed to leave the country and abandon politics.
"Pakistan is my home and I am going to live in my home," said Bhutto, who denies any wrongdoing.
The Supreme Court ruled last week that there was enough evidence to justify Leghari's action in sacking Bhutto.
Zardari has been under detention since Bhutto's dismissal on November 5 and faces a charge of conspiring to kill Murtaza.
